value.overview: The Ruddy Turnstone (Arenaria interpres) is a compact shorebird recognized by its short, slightly upturned bill, orange legs, bold black-and-white head pattern, and contrasting rufous back in breeding plumage. It breeds in Arctic and subarctic regions and spends the nonbreeding season along shorelines on most continents. The species gets its name from its habit of turning over stones, seaweed, shells, and other debris to uncover small prey.
value.classification: The Ruddy Turnstone belongs to the order Charadriiformes and the sandpiper family Scolopacidae. It is one of the two living species in the genus Arenaria.
value.identification: Adults are stocky, short-legged shorebirds measuring about 21–26 cm long. They have a stout, wedge-shaped bill, orange legs, a white belly, and a distinctive black breast band. Breeding birds show rich chestnut and black upperparts with a strongly patterned face; nonbreeding birds are duller brown. In flight, white wing bars, a white back stripe, and a broad white rump help distinguish them. Juveniles are brownish with pale feather edges.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Turnstone has a nearly worldwide distribution. It breeds on Arctic tundra, often near rocky coastlines, gravel flats, or wetlands, and winters mainly on ocean beaches, rocky shores, mudflats, estuaries, mangroves, salt ponds, and other intertidal habitats. In Costa Rica it is a regular nonbreeding visitor, occurring on both Pacific and Caribbean coasts, generally more locally and in smaller numbers on the Caribbean side. It favors sandy or rocky beaches, estuaries, mudflats, and coastal wetlands.
value.migrationStatus: It is a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, birds commonly pass through during spring migration from late March to late May and autumn migration from August to October. Some remain through the northern winter, especially along the Pacific coast, while a smaller number may remain during the northern summer without breeding. Costa Rica is not a breeding area for this species.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place during the short Arctic summer. Pairs usually nest on open tundra, gravelly ground, or coastal flats, placing a shallow nest scrape among stones, moss, or sparse vegetation. The female generally lays several well-camouflaged eggs, and both adults participate in incubation and defense. Chicks are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching, feeding themselves while being guarded by the adults. No regular breeding is known in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Ruddy Turnstones eat insects, crustaceans, mollusks, marine worms, small fish, and other shoreline invertebrates. Their strong bill is used to flip stones, shells, seaweed, driftwood, and debris, exposing hidden prey. They also probe wet sediment, pick food from rocks, and seize organisms in shallow water. In Costa Rica, they forage mainly across intertidal beaches, mudflats, estuaries, rocky shores, and coastal wetlands.
value.behavior: Ruddy Turnstones are active, alert foragers that move quickly along the waterline and frequently probe or overturn objects. They may feed alone, in pairs, or in small groups and often associate with other shorebirds. When disturbed, they give sharp calls and fly rapidly, showing their conspicuous white wing markings. They roost communally above the high-tide line, on rocks, sandbars, beaches, or other undisturbed coastal sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is declining. The total population is estimated at roughly 750,000–1,750,000 mature individuals, although estimates remain difficult because much of the breeding range is remote.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss and degradation of coastal wetlands, disturbance at migration and wintering sites, coastal development, pollution, reduced food availability, and climate-related changes affecting Arctic breeding areas and shorelines. Recreational activity, unleashed dogs, artificial lighting, and intensive use of beaches can disrupt feeding and roosting birds in Costa Rica and elsewhere.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore beaches, estuaries, mangroves, mudflats, and other coastal wetlands. Keep dogs under control near shorebird roosts, avoid disturbing concentrated flocks, respect protected-area closures, reduce plastic and chemical pollution, and support coastal development that preserves intertidal feeding and high-tide roosting habitat. Reporting sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs can help track migration and population changes.
